Corundum. Aluminium oxide—a mineral second in hardness only to diamond. It forms in metamorphic rocks and certain igneous settings, especially at high temperatures. The transparent red variety is called ruby, while all other colours, including blue sapphire, are termed sapphire. Corundum's extraordinary hardness makes it valuable both as a gemstone and as an industrial abrasive.

Corundum is rated nine on the Mohs hardness scale, second only to diamond. That's hard enough to cut or polish every other mineral except diamond itself. It forms beautiful hexagonal crystals, and its transparency and colour depend on trace elements and impurities. Ruby is red corundum, coloured by chromium. Sapphire is blue, coloured by iron and titanium, but corundum also comes in yellow, pink, and orange.

Fine rubies can command higher prices per carat than diamonds because of their rarity. Corundum forms primarily in metamorphic rocks like marble and schist, where aluminium-rich protoliths are heated and compressed. It also appears in some alumina-rich igneous rocks. For industrial purposes, synthetic corundum, or alumina, is manufactured at scale for use in grinding wheels, sandpaper, and polishing compounds.

Diamond ranks ten on the hardness scale with corundum at nine—they dominate the top of the Mohs scale. Quartz, at hardness seven, is much softer and is easily scratched by corundum. Most natural corundum forms in metamorphic rocks like marble and corundum schist. Ruby and sapphire are among the most valued gemstones, and in fine specimens they often command prices exceeding diamonds.
